At last!  COLLAPSE is that rare book - a study of environmental impact on past and present societies that does not resort to shopworn doomsday cliches.  Rather, Jared Diamond offers engaging, thoughtful analysis of many societies scattered across the globe.  Far from an indictment of man, the book offers logical explanations of how cultural, technological, religious, economic and other societal structures combine to foster long-term success or accelerate ultimate collapse.Professor Diamond examines such diverse societies as modern Montana, Easter Island, Norse Greenland, China, Rwanda and Australia (among others).  Themes are similar - lack of stewardship.  Those societies, which have collapsed, were those who sought to exploit the land for today, rather than engage in continuous and balanced renewal.  The causes range from benign neglect and ignorance, cultural restrictions and collective self-denial to exploitative opportunism.Despite its length, the book flows well and leads to reflective hope that we can - by working together - avoid the mistakes of the past without resorting to antagonistic adversarialism.  Lest, in the words of Percy Bysshe Shelley: "Nothing beside remains.  Round the decay of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretch far away."

Although I greatly admired Geraldine Brooks' earlier novel,YEAR OF WONDERS(despite its slightly rabbit-from-the-hat ending), I was wary of starting this one, since I knew its title character, March, was based upon the absent father in Louisa May Alcott'sLITTLE WOMEN, a book that I have not read. I need not have worried; Brooks' novel stands confidently by itself and supplies any back-story that is necessary. I have always been put off (perhaps in my ignorance) by what seemed an aura of Victorian sentimentalism surrounding the Alcott books, so when MARCH began with a letter home from the battlefield written in exactly this vein, I almost threw it down. But again I need not have worried; the general tone of MARCH is far from sentimental; one of its major themes, indeed, concerns what CANNOT be said in a letter home, and the unbearable pressures and unintended dishonesties which result from the wholesome desire not to bring pain to those one loves. Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy may be safe with their mother Marmee in their simple home in Concord, but the experiences of their father further South are anything but a children's tale.Brooks wries that her novels are about "faith and catastrophe"; this was true of THE YEAR OF WONDERS, but it comes much closer to home here. While ostensibly filling in the story of the fictional March father from LITTLE WOMEN, absent with the Union army in the Civil War, Brooks goes way beyond some literary what-if. Extending the quasi-autobiographical nature of Alcott's book, she draws upon the real-life character of the novelist's father, Bronson Alcott, a transcendentalist philosopher, educator, and utopian idealist, the friend of Emerson and Thoreau. But since this is fiction, the character may be made younger and emotionally vulnerable, thrust into the fighting, and, even more searing for him, brought into contact with the "liberated" slaves on former plantations. The result is to expose the moral ambiguities of the war and slavery in a manner approaching the power of Edward Jones'THE KNOWN WORLD, and test the emotional honesty and moral courage of this noble but imperfect man of peace almost to breaking point.A rich and complex book, highly recommended. For further discussion, see my review of E. L. Doctorow'sTHE MARCH.

This is a very unique story of a woman who found her true calling in life. And she knew she had found her path because there, against all circumstances, she found lasting joy.The story is very well told. At more than one juncture my eyes were moist as the authors brought out the beauty and power of one life lived wholly unto God. And their work is done transparently, so that the logical flow is clear and you can almost see the researched parts being put together.The basic story is that an upper-middle class American woman, twice divorced, approaching middle age, pursues her charitable work right into a very seamy Mexican jail. It's the improbability of the thing, each step of the way, that makes the tale so remarkable.First, because the woman was divorced and remarried, for 25 years she couldn't receive Communion from her Roman Catholic Church. Ironically, it was her second divorce that enabled her to resume the sacrament, because it was the second marriage itself that the church would not recognize.Second, once she had found the jail she wanted to work at, because of her age and her two divorces she couldn't find an order of nuns that would accept her.Those obstacles would have daunted almost anyone. But here is where the story gets priceless. Up against the wall, this indomitable woman simply stitched together her own makeshift nun's habit and walked into the jail as a member of her own religious order, praying she wouldn't be discovered!Call it functional Protestantism, and in this world of inane rules and mind-numbing regimentation, file it away, but not too deeply, for future use!Aside from her taking matters into her own hands when necessary, the other thing I really liked about this story was how Mary Clarke was led to her destiny. She started in little ways to do what she found rewarding: charitable work for the less fortunate. Then, at each juncture where a new opportunity arose, she said yes to increased service. One door opened after another, and she ended up walking into a very rare situation where she could flow deeply in God's love for people.Add to that the stories of repentant drug dealers and murderers, dirt-poor people receiving life-changing medical care, lives turned around, etc, and you have one very unforgettable tale.The irony, predictably, is that Mother Antonia now swims in plaudits from her church, even up to the Pope. But I guess that's often the way it is, and maybe has to be, as the struggle against all odds causes us to trust in and rely on God alone, and not man. This indeed is how most of the great Bible heroes were raised up.An inspiration for all, very well told. It made me draw nearer to the Lord to ask for increased consecration. Read this book. Really.

reviewText: This book has great humor and her description of places and her thinking is impeccable. BUT, with that being said, her trip to India took forever and could've been shortened in the book.  I liked her open mindedness to other belief systems and opportunities. I wish she would've described more of the love with Felipe to balance out the lust factor. I like the colorful people she meets, esp. Richard from Texas. Overall, with the exception of India's chapters going on forever, I love this book and feel it is a great read.

I am almost finished reading this book and thought someone needed to throw in a positive comment since most of the recent ones are so negative.I have read reviews on other sites as well and a lot of people, myself included, have said they could really relate to some of her relationship experiences and were truly inspired by her journey and travels. This is her life for crying out loud, so to be so opinionated about her experience is baffling!How can you fault her for her "American self -absorption?" Of course we have a different perspective that other countries. And I'm not saying that's a good thing, it just is. So, if other cultures have a better outlook, why not travel and learn other better ways to be?She readily states that she was in a time of deep emotional crises and so like most of us, keeps having all the repetitive  "Why me's?" that keep coming up at times like these. Yes you question yourself, over everything, over and over and over again. It's the human condition, people.And so, whoever finds fault with the process she had to go through, well, "Congratulations on the Enlightenment, Sister. Happy for ya!"I have been studying Buddhist meditation for 3 years. It is a hard thing to do and not just some woo-woo, hippy-dippy dancing around the Maypole exercise. Sitting with your thoughts in silence for days on end is not pretty. It is hard, cathartic, and can be liberating if you are dedicated to the practice. I'm betting most of these naysayer's wouldn't last 5 minutes attempting this!It's too bad the folks who didn't bother to read past the first few chapters, as they missed her passage into peace, happiness and compassion.Of course, it was all directed inward at first that was the whole point! That was her inspiration for setting off on this journey and the fact she was already a successful writer and was given a book advance gave her the means to do this. Which she says was the not case with her travels in the earlier in her life.Just prior to this I read "Three Cups of Tea" a truly amazing book about another person's experience coming through trials and tribulations to a place of peace and helping others. The co-author David Relin, was also criticized for his writing style which myself and others found to easy to read, considering all the drama Greg Mortenson found himself in.I cans see that her writing style can be almost too conversational at times, with lots of things in parentheses and caps, but again she was emphasizing her life and the torrent of thoughts during this time.It's one thing to just not have an interest in the storyline but quite another to be so ruthless about someone sharing their innermost journey.I'm betting all those nasty folks would never have the balls to publish their life story and then have your personal struggles bashed by the whiny self-righteous public!!Go back to reading trite bodice-ripper's if you don't want to hear all the raw, messy, beautiful stories of another person's REAL life!

Michael Pollan's "The Omnivore's Dilemma" traces four meals from their origins to the table.  In doing so, he brings to light the decisions we face each time we make a decision about our food.  Cheap chicken breasts from the local supermarket?  A trip to Whole Foods for free-range chickens?  Or a purchase from the farmers' market to support a local farmer?What makes "The Omnivore's Dilemma" come alive is Pollan's masterful voice.  He incorporates scientific findings with a personal narrative, offering a compelling journey through America's food system.  Much of the information I already knew, having grown up in a rural agricultural area -- corn is massively subsidized, beef cattle are sent to feedlots to stuff themselves on cheap corn, our whole conventional agricultural system rests on a sea of fossil fuels from the Middle East.What Pollan does so well is to weave these disparate elements to create a cohesive narrative.  He explored Big Organic (hint: the stuff you buy at Whole Foods is often shockingly similar to what's found at the local supermarket) and a small, independent farmer practicing more sustainable agricultural management.I found the foraging piece of the book, in which Pollan hunts wild pig and gathers mushrooms, to be less compelling than the rest.  Perhaps because I grew up in an area where such things were the norm, this "city slicker wrestles with guilt about killing an animal, finds out that he likes it, and succumbs to feelings of shame" bit didn't resonate with me.Overall, this is a smart book that illustrates everything that is wrong (and a few things that are right) about American food practices.  I highly recommend it to anyone wondering where their food truly comes from.
summary: A Thoughtful Account of Modern Food Production

reviewText: I haven't read all the books out there on Wal-Mart, but if this one is the best one, then someone else needs to get cracking.  I bought this book because a reviewer said that it does for Wal-Mart what "Fast Food Nation" did for Fast Food.  I have used FFN in several of my courses, and "The Wal-Mart Effect" is not in the same league.  It is written in a journalistic style, without often really digging into the questions proposed.  Fishman only briefly deals with the body of academic (and other) literature out there on this topic, and if one is seeking a careful, analytical treatment of Wal-Mart, one won't find it here.On the other hand, the steady stream of stories about Wal-Mart, and the few attempts at nailing down the facts, do have a strong, persuasive effect, even if one is, like myself, more interested than Fisher is in what we really can and do know about Wal-Mart's impact.  Fishman's punchline is that Wal-Mart is a different breed of company, and we need to treat it differently.  It sounds like a simple statement, but Fishman does fine work in making this a serious idea.  For instance, he is incredulous that Wal-Mart refuses to submit even basic information to academic researchers trying to scientifically measure Wal-Mart's impact on America.  How are we supposed to know what to do about Wal-Mart if the company won't even release information like the location and opening dates of its stores?  How are we supposed to understand the impact that Wal-Mart has on its suppliers when Wal-Mart won't release this info?  These are the issues that interest Fishman, far more than the 'traditional' Wal-Mart issues like wages, benefits, unions, loss of US jobs, etc.  I would have preferred far more on these latter issues, to the point that if I had to do it again, I would keep shopping rather than buy this book.  But if you don't know much about Wal-Mart, and don't like difficult reading, this might make a fine introduction to the Wal-Mart effect.  For a certain audience, I highly recommend this book.

Theodore Westhusing.  Westhusing's confrontation with Patraeus is the first chapter of Christian T. Miller's book Blood Money.  Listening to Gross and Ricks I was waiting for some reference to Westhusing since he had quickly identified the fiasco.  I fetched my copy of Rick's Fiasco, previously read and not fully digested.  Westhusing lived the fiasco in Iraq and blamed the Generals for letting it get out of hand.  Specifically Patraeus whom Ricks lauds.  Westhusing, was assigned the task of training Iraq's security forces in a war that none of the Generals and certainly not the Commander-in-Grief, George W. Bush and his minions.... Cheney and Rumsfeldt... considered needing a peacekeeping, anti-insurgency nor exit-stragedy. Westhusing, the cream of the "middle management" crop, trained in the Greek Classics, knowledgable of tragedy and lessons of Belisarius and an ethics professor at West Point, has no reference in Ricks' index. reviewText: There are six stories in this book, each roughly tied to the others. They are I Love Dollars; A Hospital Night; A Boat Crossing; Wheels; Ah, Xiao Xie; Pounds, Ounces, Meat.I read quite a bit of Chinese fiction, from classic to very modern. I like most of what I read. I read quite a bit of post-modern and like most of it as well. This book, though, is nearly impossible to review. Usually such a book has a few good stories, a few stinkers and the rest so-so. To me, each of these had moments of all three.Some were clever in concept but way overworked - the fallacy that if some is good then more is necessarily better. Some were a mixture of noirish post-modernism (and just quirky) that just didn't work. All had humorous moments; all had interesting characters; but none were great from beginning to end.Unless you are determined to sample untried authors, I'd give this one a pass. There were enough interesting moments to give this three stars - but had this been a novel, I'm not sure I would have finished it.

"In the Woods" can be summarized as a book with three acts.Act I superbly sets up an interesting and even compelling mystery. One of the best openings I have ever read. The heart-rending murder of a child seems to promise a deep and appropriate cause commensurate with the magnitude of the crime.But then Ms. French runs out of gas. Act II is a tedious bore going nowhere and featuring the wimpish hero's drunkeness and smoking as time fillers.And Act III is an anti-climatic disappointment of the first order. After beginning a seeming epic of evil, the perp turns out out to be motivated by the most banal of motives. The murder of a little girl is trivialized and the excellent build-up ruined.And dont even get me started on the author's cheating the reader by leaving the other major mystery unresolved. Indeed, the author spends an inordinate amount of time telling us about the personal life of her detective. One would expect this to have something to do with the two mysteries she constructs. It does not.In sum, a mystery that promises much and delivers little.
summary: A book in three acts--CAUTION: SPOILERS.

reviewText: Al Gore believes that our Enlightenment legacy of reason and self-government faces a catastrophic threat from television, greedy corporations and George W. Bush.  As primary evidence that reason and logic no longer inform our public decision making, the former Vice-President cites the lack of debate over the decision to invade Iraq.  However, Mr. Gore seems to have forgotten the lively debate which took place across a variety of media including print, television, the internet, yard signs and bumper stickers. Mr. Gore seems to believe that because the public debate failed to reach the right result that it did not occur. This is symptomatic of the problem with this book.  The Assault on Reason should be titled Why Everything Would Have Been Better If I Was President.  Mr. Gore's discussion of the role of reason in society is shallow and serves primarily as an excuse to discuss his complaints with the Bush administration.Mr. Gore's view that logic plays a diminished role in society is based in part on a nostalgic view of a past that never existed.  One of Mr. Gore's central themes is that for democracy to work, there must be two way communications between voters and government.  In Mr. Gore's view, most political communication today takes place through television, which is a one-way medium.  The former Vice-President believes that we had a more reasoned and authentic democracy in the late 18th century when political discourse took place through print media such as books, newspapers and pamphlets.  In Mr. Gore's view, the average citizen, like Thomas Paine, was able to go out and print a pamphlet when he wanted to communicate with his fellow citizens.  While the 18th century produced some great political writings, such as Common Sense and the Federalist Papers, the likelihood is that the average citizen, especially the frontiersman living on the edge of civilized society, was more likely to be a recipient of written communication than an initiator of it.Today's world of internet, print, TV and radio media offers far more avenues for both receiving and conveying information than at any other time in our history.  History will no doubt show that more people communicate through blogs today than ever wrote a political pamphlet or letter to a newspaper during the 18th century.  We also live in an age where education is much higher and leisure time is much greater.  These factors make it more probable that logic and reason play a greater role in today's society than in the past.  While the former Vice-President chooses to focus on the role of 30 second television ads, he mistakenly assumes that this is the sum and substance of the political conversation.  Voters are not robots who respond automatically to programming received from the television.  Although I don't have the evidence for this, I suspect that voters are more likely to base their decisions on conversations with friends and family than to make decisions in solitude based on TV ads.  Mr. Gore's thesis about the death of reason gives too much credence to technology and not enough credit to interpersonal relations.Mr. Gore's dirge with regard to the death of reasoned citizen involvement also overlooks the major changes which have occurred in society during that time.  There were only 38,818 votes cast in the presidential election of 1789, reflecting approximately 1% of a population of three million.  During the presidential election of 2004, there were 122 million votes cast out of a population approaching 300 million.  In the days of the founding fathers, the right to vote was limited to white property owning males (thus explaining why only 1% of the population was able to vote).  When the franchise is confined to an educated near-oligarchic minority, the quality of each individual voter's reasoned contribution is greatly increased.  Today, with a broad right to vote and a population which has grown 100 times, the average voter has less ability to impact the national or even local political discussion.  However, that does not mean that reason plays less of a role now than then.  It simply means that instead of being ruled by a narrow class of gentleman farmers, we are subject to the collective wisdom and common sense of the masses.The other major misguided theme in this book is that the presidency of George W. Bush poses a grave threat to the future of the republic.  Nearly every chapter contains a lengthy exposition of the horrors wrought by the current administration.  However, there is little context here.  The misdeeds of the Bush administration are magnified, while other crises in American history are minimized.  To read Mr. Gore's book, Americans live in a police state where all communications are monitored,  information is tightly controlled and citizens are arrested and detained without cause.  While Mr. Gore theorizes about the fact that political opponents could be declared to be  "unlawful enemy combatants" (a legal classification created in a World War II-era Supreme Court opinion rather than invented by President Bush) and detained on political grounds, he ignores the fact that actual political prosecutions occurred under the Alien and Sedition Acts. Warrantless surveillance of conversations between Americans and suspected terrorists overseas represents a small extension of constitutional boundaries, while President Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus during the Civil War was a direct assault on the Constitution.  The internment of foreign nationals at Guantanamo certainly cannot compare to the round-up of Japanese Americans during World War II. Compared to the historical record, the infractions of the current administration are Bush-league at best.  While Mr. Gore has identified extensions of Presidential power which are unhealthy and unwise, he seems to forget that the Constitution has a built-in antidote to such shenanigans.  Despite the Voldemort-like powers ascribed to the Bush administration, voters changed control of Congress in 2006.  Regardless of the considerable imagination and energy of Karl Rove, Dick Cheney and Donald Rumsfeld, the Bush administration will leave office in January 2009.  Mr. Gore's obsession with the man who defeated him for president distorts his analysis and ensures that this book will become dated once a new administration takes office.The Assault on Reason contains a confusing mish-mash of Al Gore's theories about the degraded role of reason in society and extended rants about his disagreements with the Bush administration.  It seems that the author could not make up his mind which of two books to write and did not allow an editor to clarify his thoughts. Finally on page 185, he ties it all together by explaining that if America employed reason, it would choose his preferred positions and reject the Bush administration's policies.  Al Gore the technocrat seems to have forgotten that democracy is based on the participation of many different people, not just those who agree with him.  The citizens participating in our democratic experiment have a wide variety of interests and values.  Even if they employed perfect reason, their varied backgrounds would result in a plethora of opinions.  For Mr. Gore to assume that the American people would agree with him if they just made better use of logic is shockingly arrogant.  Mr. Gore would do better to focus his energies on persuading people that his positions are wise than bemoaning the fact that they are too unreasoned to agree with him.

Saving CeeCee Honeycutt  is a warm and charming novel that will steal your heart. It is chock full of quirky and zany characters as well as strong and heartfelt ones and all are women. Cee Cee is a twelve year old girl struggling to care for her mentally ill mother in Ohio in the late 1960's. She has an absent father who travels with his job but just can't deal with the situation at home and barely knows what is going on. Cee Cee's mother continues to get worse and her behavior is humiliating and mortifying to Cee Cee. Cee Cee has no friends and is teased over her mothers antics. The only true friend Cee Cee has is an elderly neighbor who looks out for her and takes care of her.Sadly, there is a tragic accident and Cee Cee loses her mother.  Cee Cee Cee is saved by her great aunt Tootie whom she has never met and takes her to live with her in Savannah, Georgia. Aunt Tootie truly is the epitome of a southern woman and lovingly immerses Cee Cee into the world of the south and  southern women. CeeCee is taken under the wing of Aunt Tooties wonderful cook and friend Oletta and learns to love and trust again.I absolutely loved Saving CeeCee Honeycutt and I believe it will be one of my favorite books of the year. It is full to the brim with southern charm, strong and independent women, humor and heartwarming strength. I loved the sweetness and goodness in Cee Cee and she learned to protect that in herself. The women are of different races and backgrounds and so many of them were wise and outright funny. She learns from the strong women that surround her that she may have lost her mother but she has gained many more to guide her along the path of life.  I found the wisdom and quotes shared very true to life and made me want to stop and write down quite a few to remember. This novel focuses on the power of love and acceptance and how important it is to let go of the past and soar towards the future. Learning to love ourselves, believe in ourselves and trusting others can happen more easily when we let go of the things that can haunt us.I believe that Saving CeeCee Honeycutt will be a winner this year and it is a book to watch. I can't recommend it highly enough. Make sure to grab a copy as it will be out today, January 12th in bookstores. It is already garnering great raves and reviews as a debut novel by Beth Hoffman. It was chosen as the first pick for Sam's Club brand new book club. That is quite an honor and one that is well deserved.
summary: A warm and charming novel that will steal your heart!

The titular words are a quote from the novel. It begins with the recollections of Francis "Frank" Mackey about a pivotal event when he was nineteen. Late one December night he slipped out of his miserable Dublin home for a rendezvous with his lover, Rosie Daly. They planned to elope, leaving for London. But she never showed, and Frank never saw her again. He found a note from her which seemed to indicate that she was dumping him and leaving alone. Likely, she had crossed into England and never looked back, cutting off contact with her own unhappy family and her cold, tyrannical father.Twenty-two years have passed; Frank has married and divorced. Now, he's an undercover detective for "the Guard," the Dublin police. The very suitcase surfaces that Rosie took with her that fateful December night, and it's fully packed. This leads Frank to hunt for Rosie.  What follows is a most suspenseful crime story. It's also a brilliant study of family dynamics.Frank has a large family with large problems. That's why he had been willing to run away to London. He hates his abusive father, and has very few warm feelings for his mother and older brother. It seems Frank is surrounded by hard-drinking people who get mean(er) when they're drunk. They are profane and violent. Crude and rude. And hanging over it all is a dreary culture of poverty.Author Tana French is a master wordsmith. She has great insight into what makes humans tick, both on the dark and bright side. She looks at the Mackey family and the other key characters up close and personal. She has Frank tell the story himself, and Frank casts grave doubts on his own character. The reader wonders if Frank has indeed been driven insane by his own twisted family.Most highly recommended.
summary: 'Nobody in This World Can Make You Crazy Like Your Family Can"

The author makes a very convincing argument that it was the inept leadership of the United Nations and the reluctance of the US to put soldiers in the field that directly led to the Srebrenica massacre in the summer of 1995. As one of the worst cases of modern genocide, this slaughter of over 8000 Muslims has many faces. It is Rohde's thesis that this tragedy happened because of a number of interconnected decisions made inside and outside Bosnia that reflected a consciously callous betrayal of the right of an ethnic group to defend itself against hostile action. This study handles this whole sorry event as to its origin, its principals, and its terrible outcome. While the UN Security Council failed, because of some internal dissent, to secure the critical air strikes to protect the Muslim enclave from the Bosnian Serbs and their Serbian brethren, most of the blame lies with the cold-blooded efforts of two leaders to commit genocide: Karadzic, President of the Bosnian-Serb republic and Mladic, his general. Though there is a history of intense hatred between Slavic and Muslim forces in this region, the summer of 1995 definitely gave the Bosnian-Serbs the opening they were looking for to overrun a vastly outnumbered, underarmed and poorly defended Muslim city. A lot of this narrative involves the valiant efforts of a small brigade of Dutch marines who were saddled with the impossible task of keeping the enemy out of this so-called safe zone. Rohde does a capable job, with the use of reliable civilian witnesses, in showing how the massacre likely took place under cover during a UN withdrawal. For Rohde this whole fiasco could have been avoided if the UN had ordered NATO aerial attacks on Bosnian-Serbian positions around Srebrenica.

reviewText: It's the 20th installment of Donna Leon's Commissario Guide Brunetti and like a good Tuscan wine, this series seems to age well.  In "Drawing Conclusions," Leon's intrepid policeman, "shrewd, sophisticated, and compassionate,"  returns once more to attempt to put salvation back into the soul of his beloved Venice.  It's an uphill struggle, but Brunetti's resolve is never defeated--shaken, perhaps, at times, as he faces the insidious corruption that Venice (and apparently all Italy!) seems to be borne with.We've seen this struggle beginning with Leon's first Brunetti ("Death at La Fenice" in 1992).  Since then, variations on the same theme run through these episodes.  To Brunetti, hope springs eternal.Once more, the Brunetti "gang" is here, Vice Questore Patta (his albatross) and his Lieutenant Scarpa, Brunetti's trusty Inspector Vianello, Signorina Ellatra (Brunetti's more than valuable reception/computer wiz), his wife Paula, and his two children.  In Drawing Conclusions, however, Leon turns to introspection, to Brunetti's ethics, his brilliant deductions, his code of honor deep inside him, to carry the story.  Leon depends less upon the supporting cast and concentrates on our Brunetti.  And this is well and good. The reader really does get to know more about what makes Brunetti Brunetti. This shift in pattern happens to be a good one--well, for now, at any rate (we do want to see more of the other characters in later works, as well as some more of her food menus!).As the story goes, "An old woman's body has been found in a Spartan apartment on Campo San Giacomo dell'Orio. Her neighbor discovered it when she went to pick up her mail, after having been away in Palermo."Brunetti  is called and, of course, after seeing the medical examiner rule that the old woman has died of a heart attack, there perhaps isn't anything that should involve him, afterall.  Ahh.  But Brunetti has this nagging feeling that something is amiss. And, of course,  there is something amiss.  As he suspects, a murder is involved.  Now, we find Brunetti at his best and it's only a matter of time before he, and his team, defying odds, both political and criminal, solve the case.  Getting there is the spell-binding part, though, in true Leon fashion.  Her publisher writes that "Drawing Conclusions" is "insightful and emotionally powerful."  This may not be the best Brunetti, but it's certainly one of the best.  It's nice to see Leon continuing this worthy series.

Marie Antoinette's Swedish lover, Count Axel Von Fersen, is cast in this historical novel in the type of John F. Kennedy. Good looking, powerful, and with a string of beautiful woman dangling from his fingers. This is the story of how Count Axel was tied to the royal family by his love of Marie Antoinette, attempted to help them escape, and finally observed their demise from his various posts throughout Europe. Having fought in the American Revolution, the Count disdained American society and economy. He was an aristocrat of the ruling class, disinterested in politics that did not favor the preservation of royalty. This novel was thoroughly researched with the details of a careful eye: pets, textures, colors, a way of walking, turns of phrases, and culinary delights.The novel is written from two perspectives: Axel's personal diary, and his sister who found the diary and inserted chapters where the diary goes blank.Count Axel is an unlikely hero. You don't want to like him. You want to disdain him for his womanizing. On the very eve when he bid "Toinette" farewell for the very last time, he immediately ran into the arms of another lover. I did not have a sense of what motivated him to make the choices he did, of what drove him, of what he ultimately wanted out of life.The author does a remarkable job of painting the political scene of the time period - the Revolution, the buttons with "Live Free or Die" on the coats of soldiers, the decapitation of servants, the shrinking of the Queen while imprisoned, and even the wish of King Louis not to bid farewell to his family on the morning he was guillotined. The politics of the novel are explained well, clearly and succinctly.The expected cast is all in attendance: Robespierre, the fat and messy King Louis XVI, the love child of Antoinette and Axel (the third in line of the royal family), and even the cast of the Affair of the Necklace - Jeanne de La Motte, Cardinal de Rohan, and the jeweler Monsieur Bohmer.I relish this time period, and this story. While I enjoyed the critical eye to detail, I wish there was more character development. Very little detail of how and why Antoinette fell in love with Count Axel was given. We see precious little of the queen's thoughts, mostly given in letters she sent to the Count or to supporters. I wish there was more about why Toinette was so special to a ravenous womanizer like Axel. He did not shrink from being with other women on the same day he was with the Queen. Why would he go to such lengths if he truly loved her, as he professed to do? Was he just human, or not so much in love that he could deny himself?The writing is excellent, the details careful and meticulous, and the time period carefully constructed. A wonderful piece!

The use of cliches throughout the book was also overwhelming and gives the sense of a simplistic writing style.I found the main character to be dull and very anti-social; However, after one twist in the story, everything changed and she seemed to completely turn around (in the last 10-15 pages). The dialogue of one of the secondary characters, and an inhabitant of the house, left something to be desired. Her speech was written in such a way that it was supposed to imply an accent and English as her second language but it didn't come across that way in the writing. Instead, it made her seem as though she was of less than average intelligence and a bit child-like.Overall, the story line was there even though I felt it was still in the beginning phases. And I have to give credit for the ability to make a (usually) inanimate object a main character in the story. The house itself was the most in-depth character there was.

Having read "The Pillars of the Earth" earlier this year, I didn't wait long to pick up this volume.  The first three hundred pages were very reminiscent of the first book, but then it came into its own.  Contrary to the few reviewers on this site who panned the book as dull and its characters as poorly developed, I enjoyed the book thoroughly.  In fact, this 60 year old college professor was very sad when the book ended.  I felt like I had lived the main characters lives with them and that I knew them like friends or relatives.  Yes, Follett inserted many anachronisms in speech and sensibility.  But the book makes you realize the humanity of those who lived in those days and the constraints they lived under.  The two main characters - Merthin and Caris - are very unusual in their times.  However, that makes them stand out in as individuals.  Most of their peers believed in spirits and potions.  The medieval doctors in the book believed in humors and bleeding, beliefs that lasted into the 18th century.  But there must have been many skeptics during this century, like the two protagonists.  To follow up on the novel, I'm re-reading Chaucer's "Canterbury Tales," written later in the 14th century in which "World Without End" takes place.  The number of lecherous monks, adulterous wives and libidinous episodes is rather high in Chaucer.  The sophistication of the people narrating Chaucers "Tales" correlates well with the advanced consciousness of Follett's characters.  But Follett is writing in the 21st century, for us.  His novel speaks to us and is not intended to be limited to what was current thinking in 1360.  He is a great storyteller.  If you can't enjoy this book, I feel sorry for you.
summary: Why did it have to end? Great book!

Of the many reviews I have read, I think the most common two complaints are that the language is too modern, and the descriptions of medieval life are too detailed, getting down to the process by which certain items are made.  The long and short of it is this:  A book written in the linguistic style of 12th Century England would not be as accessible to modern readers.  "Pillars of the Earth" allows readers to enjoy an excellent story, set in a trying time period, full of rich detail that allows the reader to identify with the trials experienced by commoner and high-born alike, without having the difficulty that every high schooler experiences the first time they pick up a Shakespearean play, written 4 centuries after the period in which this book is set.  The characters are generally either Good or Bad, but each has their own set of flaws and virtues, which add depth to the narrative.  The religious references are frequent, but add to the story, rather than detract from it, and reflect much of the prevailing opinions of the time, both negative and positive.  Follett has done an excellent job of researching his setting and characters to be true to the time period, without his narrative being so true to the time period as to be useless in this one.
summary: A Medieval Setting With Modern Accessibility

reviewText: Ken Follett's agent, Al Zuckerman, told Follett not to publish Pillars until he had made a name for himself with his other books.  Why?  Because the story didn't have enough of the necessary six creative writing elements to make it a bestseller.  (According to Zuckerman they are: high stakes, larger than life characters, a clear dramatic foundation, an outlandish premise, multiple points of view, and captivating settings.)  And this is not from a critic but from Follett's biggest cheerleader, his agent. The lack of high stakes alone would have tanked this book's chances had Follett not already established a loyal readership for himself.  Also, Follett's writing style in this book is droning, and it is crafted with the lowest common denominator in mind, with simple words, constructions, and absense of subtelties. The language is so simplistic that it often reads more like an English translation of a foreign novel.  It is also not tight; it rambles with scenes unnecessary to the plot or character development.  Yet, eleven years after its publication, and now bearing the Oprah seal of approval, it remains in the top 100 books sold in the "thriller" category.  A loyal readership alone wouldn't have maintained this book's popularity.  Probably the ultra rich historical detail is the explanation, along with the romance between highly empathetic characters which is set amidst that historical realism.  Follett himself considers it his best novel.  It's certainly not his best written novel, though it appears that it will be his best selling novel.  In this day and age that's what counts.
summary: Only in One Sense is it Follett's Best

This is a companion volume to Mario Vargas Llosa's Feast of the Goat. Set in Santo Domingo during the Trujillo rule and after, and in New Jersey among Dominican emigrants, the 'diaspora', after Trujillo's death by assassination. The killing brought no luck to the assassins, including way up to the top of the command chain. Why else did JFK get killed but for the curse of Trujillo? (The word for the curse cannot be written here, it goes against zoo rules.)So much for history. (Santo Domingo was Iraq before Iraq was Iraq.)It is perfectly ok for you not to believe in these curses, these superstitions. They believe in you. That is enough.A book about a boy, an obese Sci-fi nerd and a suicidal loner. Oscar's problem is that he loves girls, but they don't love him. In a macho culture that makes him a sad misfit. Also a book about his sister and her mother troubles. And much about their mother, an orphan thanks to the goat, and her men troubles. And her cancer troubles. Mother and daughter share an inextinguishable longing for elsewheres.Racism is part of the plot. The family has unwhite influences. The goat had many Haitians, including their mixed race offspring, killed.The language of the main narrator is refreshingly foulmouthed, which stands in contrast to the complex narrative structure and the overload of allusions to all kinds of worlds. Also in contrast to the essentially tragic story.I am not a scifi nerd or fantasy fan myself, therefore many names are lost on me. Doesn't seem to matter much. The narrator is an involved person, but is slow to disclose his identity. Takes him about half through the novel. The explanation for the name Wao comes a few pages later. No spoilers.In two chapters, Oscar's sister Lola (a Dolores like the original Lolita) narrates, as if JD wanted to try it out. Those are, frankly, weaker. I wonder, maybe he can't plausibly impersonate a woman? He wouldn't be the first male writer with a problem in that department.I do not always agree with the Pulitzers for fiction, but this time the choice was right.I think I might have had some difficulties of comprehension had I not read the Vargas Llosa  book recently. I might even have thought it exaggerated. I might have thought the violence and cruelty of the goat year stories are part of a core of magical realism, centered around the mother's miraculous survival as a teen at home. Star of the survival story is a mongoose. I am partial to that species ever since Rikki Tikki Tavi and since I had a mongoose family as house guests in an earlier life.(JD refers to MVL in an endnote, criticizing the too sympathetic picture of Balaguer in the Feast of the Goat. He also lets the narrator mention MVL, saying that the central rape scene in Feast of the Goat was a standard occurrence in the DomRep.)

reviewText: The most tragic aspect of Stieg Larsson's early death is that his books never got a chance to achieve that final polish. Here are a pair of great characters: Mikael Blomkvist, an investigative reporter disgraced by a libel conviction, and the title character, Lisbeth Salander, an autistic computer hacker with authority issues who operates on the very edge of society.The author sets out a juicy puzzle: what happened to the missing heir of the Vanger family? How did the teenage Harriet Vanger vanish from an island on the same day that an accident closed the bridge to the mainland?Her body was never found.It's a great premise with wonderful characters, but the story unfolds in a rambling way and there are absolute issues with the writing and holes in the development, especially as book draws to a close. I can totally understand the enthusiasm which this book excites; I enjoyed reading it, but it was like reading the rough draft of a potentially great novel which misses greatness because of inconsistencies and details that don't ring true.I liked the characters enough that I will certainly read the other books in the series if they come my way; but these books probably would have been better if the author had lived to edit them into tighter form. I'd like to rate this higher: shall I say 3 and a half stars?

It is hard -- and almost unnecessary -- to add to the countless accolades that have already been conferred on the late Stieg Larsson's "Millennium" trilogy, of which "The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" is the first volume. In many regards, this first part is also the best, with what is arguably the most satisfying story lines, which follow a brilliantly structured series of arcs that make the book part political thriller, part psychological drama, part locked-room mystery and, it has to be said, a fair amount soap opera. Superbly devised plot-lines aside, the book's well-rounded and strongly developed main characters go a long way towards making the journey through this hefty tome seem much shorter than it is. The author also does a wonderful job of conveying many everyday details of life in Sweden, through the inclusion of many little mundane details - although his obsession with detailing every single technical specification of things like the characters' computing equipment does become a little tedious at times. One wonders how much tighter this manuscript might have been edited had the author lived to see that to fruition.We shall, of course, never know the answer to that question but there is no need to lose sleep over it; the book's shortcomings are minor in comparison to its many strengths.  The book may feel a little slow at the beginning, and its cast to vast and varied that it's hard to remember who everyone is sometime, but do stay with it -- once it gets going it really does provide one heck of a roller coaster ride.  It is even pretty much complete as a tale in its own right, and doesn't require the subsequent reading of the subsequent volume, "The Girl Who Played with Fire", to bring anything much to a conclusion.Strongly recommended.

reviewText: I am almost always disappointed in sequels, but this was awesome.  The world that Steig Larsson has created is so entertaining, that I could not put this book down.This story revolves around sex trafficking in Sweden and some murders that our gal Lisbeth is accused of doing.  Michael Blomkvist is back as our intreprid reporter and he is working on the sex trade story with the two people that get killed.  Lisbeth's fingerprints are on the gun and we know she was meeting with these people.  Of course, the only reason she even knows who they are is because she hacked into Michael's computer to see what was going on.In the first book it takes forever for Lisbeth and Michael to meet, in this book they don't meet again until the very end. UGH - how frustrating for me.  But of course, that was our authors intent.If you have read The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, then you know Lisbeth is angry with Michael and has cut him out of her life.  He is aware of this, yet he stands by her through these murder charges.  He is man of true depth and he really cares about Lisbeth, as do we all.  She is a great protaganist.  When she is part of the story, it just flows so quickly.  You hate to see the chapter move on to another character. We also find out so much more about Lisbeth in this book - you will be sad, shocked and angry all at the same time for her.The ending keeps you on the edge of your seat and I just couldn't wait to pick up the next story.  While that is precisely what I did, I don't recommend it unless you do not have to be up for work the next morning.I would say you don't have to read The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo before this one, I would recommend it.  It will really help you to understand who Lisbeth is and why she is a hero to so many of us out there.  Ok, hero might be an exaggeration, but I love her.  Even my 68 year old mother loves her and she is a very particular reader.Have fun all.

I had to read the last book, GIRL WHO KICKED THE HORNET'S NEST, before I could write this review.  Although it was, in the end, worth the time and frustration, I had to take several breaks while reading this installment of the trilogy.First off, there's way too much information, way too many characters.  Added to the huge cast of characters and the foreign names, Mr. Larsson switched back and forth between using a character's first name and last name.  For example; some of the names included in this trilogy are Blomkvist, Berger, Bublanski, Bjour (?spelling), and even more names beginning with the letter 'B'.  There are two Irene's.  There is a Neidermann and a Nieminen, and a town called Norrtalje.Political situations in Sweden are beyond my reach, and frankly just confused me.  Street names, what I assume are towns or colonies or whatever confused me.The spelling (misspelling) of words also bothered me.However, when I muddled through the names, and too much detail, I truly enjoyed this book and was glad I knew there was a third and final novel to wrap up all the loose ends left in this one.The three star rating comes from my personal frustration.  In the end, these books are worth the time.Shelley Dawn, author ofSweet, Sweet JessieandDark Nights

The story of the algorithm is a good one, and Berlinski can write  intelligibly about mathematics, which is rare. Unfortunately, the work-like  the Tour of the Calculus before it-is marred by the author's stylistic  excesses. Berlinski is a notorious over writer. He never met an adjective  he didn't like. His historic fantasies simply don't advance the story.  To  wit: "The duke of Brunswick, his issue destined for the British throne  but his attention fatally diverted by his screaming bladder, waggles his  pink palms, rises rapidly from his sea, and without a word scuttles down  the long library corridor of the massive wooden double doors, where, after  pulling at the red tasseled bell rope, he waits in an agony of impatience  for a footman to appear."There are similar passages on most every  page. Part One:  a child/adolescent tries to sort out which religion is the "right" religion. By the end of Part One, Pi chooses them all.Part Two: an adolescent is the sole survivor of a shipwreck.  Interrogators are sent to determine the reason why the ship sunk. In their interview they listen to the entire story that Pi has presented in Part Two -- which sounds to them like a fantasy. So, Pi gives them another story which they believe.  The interrogators never do pursue their original purpose: to determine why the ship sunk.Part Two is one big metaphor for Part One.I found myself completely disenchanted with the entire book as I plowed through it; it seemed amateurish, some of it was directly from Robinson Crusoe (both diaries ended abruptly due to running out of ink/paper), etc.Robinson Crusoe is so much more believable.And that was my attitude: plowing through the book. Drudgery. And then slam bang hit me in the face two pages near the very end that, an epiphany, explained it all. I was blown away -- after all that reading, in just two pages, I was blown away.I think that if the author had written in a more sophisticated style (like the great late 19th and early 20th century writers), the book may have appeared to be better literature. But written in an adolescent style makes sense -- it was being narrated by an adolescent.So, the book is not great literature in terms of sentence structure, vocabulary, metaphors, etc., but the way it hits you at the end will keep you thinking about it for quite some time.One question: is there more hidden in the book that I might have missed? Is it worth reading a second or a third time once one has discovered the message? It might be.But regardless, Part Two is a parable every bit as good as any parable in the Bible -- just a whole lot longer, and requires Part One as background to explain to the reader why the author wrote this book. In fact, had there been no Part One, the book would have made no sense.  Part One is crucial to understanding the message in Part Two.So, five stars for overall impact; three stars for "fun to read" as great literature. It is probably written at the 8th grade level, but its message is probably too deep for those not yet at college level reading.

Piscing Molitor Patel, otherwise known as "Pi Patel, had an inspirational story to tell a journalist about his life at sea.  It is one that can change any person's heart and make- or hope make them appreciate the finer things in life.The book and the movie are quite similar.  So if you watched the movie, then there is really no reason to read the book.  In fact, there may have been a couple more colorful additions in the movie.  Of course that is my opinion.  Yet there WERE some minute details that changed between the movie and the book, unless I wasn't paying close attention to the movie when I was watching it.Pi started his life in India, and grew very close to GOD.  There came a point where his dad thought it was necessary to sell the business, and they would be best to move the family to Canada, so they boarded ship, and this is where Pi's adventure began. The ship sunk in the midst of a storm and the only known survivor were him and Richard Parker- a Bengal Tiger.  He had to survive in a lifeboat for- I believe he said 227 days in the book. There are just so many details in the story that are so inspirational, and for him to be alive to tell the story to the journalist who is going to write Pi's story at the end of the movie is a story is touching and moving.There were moments at sea though where one would understand why Pi- a very spiritual, and God fearing, and God loving boy would have had his spirits "dampened."  He saw  quite a few storms that could have killed both him and Richard Parker, a man eating island that he thought was his sanctuary, but soon found out if he stayed much longer, he would die there, so he had to head back out to sea- that being blind faith.Read the book or watch the movie, or both to see what adventure Pi wants to bring you on.  I guarantee you will be satisfied and touched.  In fact you will be happy with what you have in front of you and the warmth and shelter that is provided for you because you never know when something may be taken away.Happy Reading.  Things may be "Irrational" at times, just like the life of "Pi" and the number "Pi."  :-)
summary: Being a Castaway at Sea Can Really DAMPEN One's Spirtits…..

This story switches between the stories of Anna Schlemmer and her daughter Trudy.  Anna does the unthinkable and violates one of the Reich's biggest prohibitions.  The resulting pregnancy thrusts Anna into a world where Anna must only think of survival.  Trudy, in a world far removed from World War II, knows nothing of her mother's past and doesn't understand why she can't surpass her mother's wall of silence.If you are looking for a story that you can disappear into, this is the story for you.  Both women are intensely affected by the effects of the war even though the women are worlds apart.  Anna manages to survive despite various ethical dilemmas, pain, and struggles with her own identity.  She wants to forget the past, whereas, her daughter needs the past for her own identity.  Very few authors manage to create a story about an era of such heartbreak and still leave the reader enthralled and wanting more.  It is deep without being too heavy or depressing.  Once you start you won't want to put it down.  After this book, you will go searching for more!

reviewText: Andrej Stasiuk, Poland`s leading literary stylist, suffers from an insatiable addiction:  travel.  Travel, that is, to those forgotten corners of Eastern Europe, those Balkan hamlets, Carpathian villages, and specks on the Hungarian plain. `Road to Babadag` is a crazed, scattered, unfocused compendium of Stasiuk`s peregrinations through the `other Europe.'Stasiuk sketches his destinations in a hazy vignette form. Whether he`s describing Rasinari, the birthplace of Romanian philosopher, Emil Cioran, ethnically contentious Transylvania, the hermit kingdom of Albania or fairy- tale Moldavia, Stasiuk`s curt, lipid prose evokes the atmosphere of these fascinating places.Stasiuk paints tantalizing, almost mystical portraits of each place.  Of Rasinari he writes, "The mountain brought the sharp, acrid smell of pens-a mélange of trampled herbs, sticky fat fleece, and dried green balls of excrement like stones."  A village in northern Hungary, "hadn`t changed in a hundred years.  Wide scattered houses under fruit trees. The walls a sulfurous, bilious yellow, the wood carving deep brown, the door frames sculpted, the shutters and verandas enduring in perfect symbiosis with the heavy Baroque abundance of the gardens."Of Baia Mare, an industrial city in the Romanian Carpathians, he muses, "Mounds of black sludge-some kind of chemical waste-gave way to mounds of containers:  polymer, cardboard, glass. Tin cans, rubber hoses, radioactive mud, cyanides from gold mines, lead and zinc, ponds of oil, soot, smoke, the final decadence of industry, all under a bright sky."  With his insistence on the concrete, Stasiuk captures the essence of each locale.Stasiuk attempts to divine the unique spiritus of each obscure destination. His writings and travels to such forlorn places originate from his obsession with,"decline, decay, to everything that is not as it could or should be."  Writing about places teetering on the brink of oblivion, he seeks to preserve their rarefied identity for generations to come.  Such preserved backwaters maintain a life-form, that apes nothing, seeks no glory and finds meaning in a centuries`s old existence.  `Road to Babadag' honors the region`s stubborn drive to exist without innovation nor progress.For the reader who has traveled many of Stasiuk`s roads, this book will bring a special delight.  He has succeeded in immortalizing places that have failed to grasp the tailcoat of Pan-European grandeur.  Of Enver Hoxha`s mountain utopia (Albania), Stasiuk speaks for all of Europe`s hidden corners.  "Albania, see, is ancient. It`s beauty brings to mind species and epochs that are long extinct and have left behind no likenesses."

Do you want your heart to be awed? Do you want to be held in suspense? Do you want to laugh and cry? Well, this book is definitely for you. The Princess Bride has many wonderful characters and like every book some evil ones.Buttercup is also later known as Princess Buttercup. Before she became a princess she lived on a farm as a milkmaid. The "Farm Boy" Wesley, always helped with anything that needed tending to. The two of them were deeply in love, but that changed when the Dread Pirate Roberts takes him on his ship to seek great riches with him. Soon Wesley is reported dead. After his untimely death the evil Prince Humperdink recognizes Buttercup's beauty and sends three men after her. Vizzini, Inigo Montoya, and Fezzik head out after her while a man in black follows them closely behind. Who is this masked man? What will happen to Buttercup and her unwanted husband?Buttercup is the heroine of the story. She is known as the most beautiful woman in the world and is in love with Wesley. Wesley is the hero of the story. He is the daring young man who boards the ship of Dread Pirate Roberts. Prince Humperdink is evil and has a lot on his mind. He wants to kill his soon to be wife, frame the Guilderians across the sea, and start a war. Vizzini is the brains behind the capture of Buttercup. He is known to be the smartest man alive. Inigo Montoya is the best swordsman in the world. His father was killed by one of Prince Humperdink's men, Count Rugen, and Inigo has been on his own personal vendetta ever since. Fezzik is a giant man, but is very caring. Fezzik used to be a champion fighter in his country and loves to rhyme. Count Rugen is Prince Humperdink's partner in crime. He has six fingers and loves torture and spends most of his time studying it.Here is a scene from the book. This is when Inigo and the Man in Black are fencing with each other.[Fencing]Inigo Montoya: You are wonderful!Man in Black: Thank you; I've worked hard to become so.Inigo Montoya: I admit it, you are better than I am.Man in Black: Then why are you smiling?Inigo Montoya: Because I know something you don't know.Man in Black: And what is that?Inigo Montoya: I... am not left-handed![Moves his sword to his right hand and gains an advantage]Man in Black: You are amazing!Inigo Montoya: I ought to be, after 20 years.Man in Black: Oh, there's something I ought to tell you.Inigo Montoya: Tell me.Man in Black: I'm not left-handed either.[Moves his sword to his right hand and regains his advantage]This is a very famous quote from the book:Inigo Montoya: Hello. My name is Inigo Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die.One more quote from the book shows some of the humor:Inigo Montoya: That Vizzini, he can *fuss*.Fezzik: Fuss, fuss... I think he like to scream at *us*.Inigo Montoya: Probably he means no *harm*.Fezzik: He's really very short on *charm*.Inigo Montoya: You have a great gift for rhyme.Fezzik: Yes, yes, some of the time.Vizzini: Enough of that!Inigo Montoya: Fezzik, are there rocks ahead?Fezzik: If there are, we all be dead!Vizzini: No more rhymes now, I mean it!Fezzik: Anybody want a peanut?Vizzini: DYEEAAHHHHHH!!After I saw the fantastic movie The Princess Bride, I sought to find if the movie was based off the book. My search was a success! I found the book. The book was written by William Goldman. I quickly read the book and was in love with it. It is better than the movie, but the movie is very well adapted and there are few changes from book to movie.I would recommend this book for young adults and up. I would give this book four stars.This book will dazzle you with its humor and suspense. The characters in a book are what make a book good and in The Princess Bride; the characters are some of the best parts.

reviewText: I can not honestly say that What Francine did was right, but I can say I can definitely see how in her pressured and stressed predicatment that she felt so trapped and let down by the system that she felt her only sure option was to burn her husband alive. I think this is a good definition of what intense and prolonged trauma can do to a human. Even the best of us can snap in a situation like that. Lenore Walker used the idea of learned helplessness and the battered woman syndrome to explain such behavior and Francine, unfortunately, demonstrated it. I can praise the spirit of survival of Francine, but we must continue to work hard to elimate the climate that would entrap victims into seeking their own solutions because the system did not provide them. Francine did the only thing she could rationally believe would work at that time. I hope and I do feel today, we all have more options.The book should be used as a continous tool as a warning of what extreme relentless trauma can do to a rational person.Torn From the Inside Out is a memoir that is similar in many ways.
summary: an example of what too much pressure for too long can do

I read this delightful tale years ago in an anthology of short stories, and was thrilled to see it available again in this lovely illustrated children's book.  This is a story to delight animal lovers of all ages.I should add here that there is really no "religious custom"  forbidding Jews to have cats (I myself have six of them!)  Appleblossom the  cat tells Naphtali that her father belongs to the rabbi's son -- and if the  rabbi's son has a cat, then it must be permitted!  This is really a story  about a father who personally doesn't care much for cats and is finding  "religious" excuses to say "No cats."  What Naphtali's  father quotes are really folk superstitions about cats -- and Naphtali's  mother seems to know that, because she wants a cat, too.  Of course, the  reader knows the story will have a happy ending -- with a little bit of  help from Elijah the Prophet (who traditionally settles deadlocked  disputes.)The watercolor illustrations are filled with light and  spirituality -- I especially love the one of Appleblossom looking down at  Naphtali from the blossoming tree branches.  The one minor  "blooper" that some Jewish families might wonder about is that  Naphtali, although clearly a religious Jew, is wearing shorts -- which was  not the custom among Jews in Eastern Europe where he is supposed to be  living.  But the illustrator herself was born in England, and British  schoolboys do traditionally wear short pants, so this can be probably  explained as being based on what she saw in her own homeland.  (Not a big  issue, but some Jewish children may wonder about it.)An excellent book  -- I'd give it ten stars if I could.  Order one now for next Passover.

I read this for the first time as a teenager, and re-read it recently. It stands up to re-reading. There are two books in this story arc, and you kind of have to take it on faith that it will all come together at the end, but it does. I think if it were published today, they might make it one solid book - each one isn't very long.If you're hoping for an in-depth story of the magic of faerie, you'll probably be disappointed. While there is magic in here, this is really a story about coming of age in a slightly gritty, youth-dominated city with the typical drug and gang problems. Reading it as an adult, the struggle and strife between young people trying to live together, make businesses work, and occasionally get married and move out to the suburbs felt pretty realistic despite the magical setting.

I mostly really like Flora. She is grating in exactly the way someone of her age would be grating to someone a lot older! Nicely written!I also love that she is not a supposedly reluctant meddler. She LIVES to meddle. And this causes all sorts of problems- and solutions- for her and for everyone else. (I have long felt a true avatar of Eris would be a teenaged girl... and probably one trying to do the Right Thing.)The romantic triangle was semi-resolved in an excellent way, but one that will clearly have implications in the future. (It is pretty clear that this trilogy is not the end of the series.) So were most of the plot threads from the previous 2 novels, though they too leave many possibilities open for future tales.The world is an interesting alternative history, sort of; it's set in a VERY alternative California, where the Aztecs are the main political power. It's intriguing but- as is true of the magical systems- our perception of the whole is choppy since it's through the eyes of a teen.Don't start here- you won't understand half the action, at least. If these books sound like fun- and they are- start with "Flora Segunda".
summary: A good not-quite-end to the trilogy

reviewText: Baltasar and Blimunda is a masterpiece of fiction, feeling and language.  History is rewritten as an ironic, sometimes painful parable for all kinds  of religious fanaticism and despotic power, where common people play a very  important role. Saramago's revolutionary writing is extremely rich in  metaphors, word games and alternative meanings. Actually, Saramago writes  poetical prose, dense at first sight, but surprisingly easy to understand  after some pages, playing with proverbs, idiomatic expressions and  intertextual passages and offering us unexpected poems, motivated by  simple, tender details.

reviewText: "Where is Joe Merchant" is a professional enough work, but one that doesn't have the wild inventiveness and manic spark of Carl Hiaasen's work or the sweet charm of Jimmy's other works. It's clearly an attempt to marry the two worlds, but if such an attempt can succeed (and I imagine someone will do it at some point), this book ain't it.In "Tales from Margaritaville," Jimmy showed that he understood the short story form, infusing his tales with characters and situations that also appear on the album "Off to See the Lizard." Lightning doesn't strike twice, though, with this work. The settings and characters seem forced rather than charming, which is a shame, as Jimmy is certainly capable of creating settings and characters to rival the TV shows "Northern Exposure" or "Ed." This time around, though, Jimmy fails to put such on paper.This is only a book worth reading by the Parrothead completist.

Beautifully written in an experimental style that sometimes reminds me of Faulkner--no paragraph indents or dialogue markings, everything just run together--this fable presents a warning against an over-reliance on technology. An aging potter, his daughter, and her husband live in a rural village. The potter's livelihood is threatened, however, when the ominous Center (kind of a combination high rise apartment and hedonistic shopping center) replaces his crockery with plastic vessels and cancels all orders. This seemingly simple story becomes more complex as the family adopts a stray dog (which they name Found) and the son-in-law plans to become a Resident Guard at the Center where they don't allow pets. The book is kind of a Luddite manifesto, dramatizing how technology and cheap machine-made products are jeopardizing artisanship and the creativity in all of us. At the same time, the book is a literary response to Plato's "Allegory of the Cave." Translated from the Portuguese, this is a read you won't soon forget--highly recommended!

Described as a busy woman's guide to igniting the writer within.This is the perfect book for individuals who want to start writing but never seem to find the time.  Stay-at-home moms may particularly find this book useful since they often can only find pockets of time for themselves.The author writes:  "Using fifteen-minute segments truly can start you on the road to becoming a writer...When (my students) give even small chunks of time to writing, incredible things begin to happen.  Resistance to writing evaporates and is replaced with a feeling of fun and discovery."Each section is extremely short (1 to 2 pages).  At the end of each section is a writing assignment.  "Set your timer" helps the reader jump start a writing activity.  If you are short on time you could read the section and then later do the assignment.One of the first assignments encourages the reader to track how she spends time and then determine where those hidden pockets of time can be found throughout the day.  The author claims that everyone has at least 15 minutes a day to write.One of my favorite activities from the book involves writing evocative words or phrases on slips of paper.  Fold the papers and put them into a small container.  Choose a word or two and set the timer for 5 minutes.  Write whatever comes into your head and don't stop until the time is up.Another idea is to collect post cards or family photos. reviewText: Scarlett Thomas has unleashed an incredibly ambitious novel here, in the form of a thought experiment encompassing vast areas of philosophy and quantum physics. Like at least one previous reviewer in this forum, I was reminded a bit of Neal Stephenson, at least thematically, in that wired-philosophical-quantum-universal-theory-of-everything sort of way. It's all wrapped up in the tale of a flawed heroine, Ariel, who is researching a supposedly cursed book that offers its few readers a recipe for entering an alternate dimension of pure thought (the Troposphere).Ariel embarks on bizarre psychosexual explorations in both the Troposphere and in the physical world, while frequently engaging in PhD-level discussions on super-advanced philosophy and relativity. This is the aspect of the book that will probably turn off many readers, as Ariel and the other characters descend into chapter-length egghead discussions, and usually right in the middle of the drama or action. Fortunately Scarlett Thomas seems to know plenty about such matters and she usually - but not always - keeps the brain exercises integrated with the plot. But I can't blame other readers for getting exasperated with the constant obscure references to Heidegger, Derrida, and Einstein - and such discussions really slow down the second half of the novel.On the good side, the general plotline surrounding the cursed book and the Troposphere is consistently fascinating, and there are some pretty good developments in Ariel's character as she compares her own messed-up life to the possibilities of living in a purely mental realm, in which she can experience the thoughts and feelings of others. The deep-thinking characters are also a bonus for bookworms and philosophically-minded readers, and I bet that Scarlett Thomas could write a believable (if very dense) non-fiction textbook on the postructuralist physics ruminated on by her characters. However, I did not care for the story's ending and Thomas has crammed way too many cosmological and epistemological (gasp!) ideas into the storyline. Regardless of Thomas's ambition, it's very difficult to keep a theory-of-the-universe thought experiment like this under control. Regardless, this is a highly unique novel for readers of a certain mindset. [~doomsdayer520~]

I consider this book as a sly satire of Baigent and Leigh's "Holy Blood Holy Grail," warning of the dangers of making too many connections between unrelated esoterica; whereas Dan Brown's book is more of a pulp popularization of the Holy Blood Holy Grail thesis.  I enjoyed DaVinci Code for what it was, and FP is still a favorite of mine; although the first 300 pages are difficult and tugid, once you get over that there's quite a payoff, as the Plan takes over and sucks you in.Read all three books and you'll be smirking along with Eco.  If not - if you're still hopped up over the Secret of the Holy Grail and other bits of two millenuim of European esoterica - listen to the audio lecture series "Western Quest" by Joseph Campbell (particularly the last three tapes) and you'll get a nice and grounded representation of what all this stuff symbolizes.  Either way, enjoy, and watch out for the Tres!
